overview: The imported name “Boihaenum” appears to refer to ancient Boiohaemum, associated with Maroboduus and the Marcomanni. Its outline lies mainly in eastern Moravia and Slovakia, poorly matching the commonly proposed Bohemian core. Neither these borders nor a continuous kingdom from 1 BCE to 300 CE are established. The examples below distinguish regional Germanic communities from Roman military installations.

periods.title: Maroboduus and his alliances
periods.summary: A powerful leader emerged around the turn of the era and lost power in 19 CE.

periods.title: Later regional communities
periods.summary: The map continues across centuries of settlement and contact with Rome, not one documented dynasty.

items.text: Roman-period settlements in Bohemia and Moravia often occupied low ground near streams and rivers. Excavations reveal houses, wells, storage pits and craft installations. These communities depended on farming and practical access to water, even when Roman writers preferred dramatic stories about warriors.

Many local buildings had rectangular floors sunk partly below ground, with posts supporting the roof. Woven branches coated in clay probably formed their walls. Archaeologists can reconstruct the plan more confidently than the vanished roof, furniture or exact number of people sleeping inside.

Food storage included underground silos and structures interpreted as raised granaries. Small farmstead groups combined homes, storage and work areas; the museum suggests that a family or small group could occupy one. A household had to keep future meals safe as well as cook today’s.

Plant remains from regional settlements include barley, wheat, millet, peas and lentils. These crops make settled cultivation visible even where ancient outsiders described people mainly as hunters. Fields, harvests and grain storage occupied a large part of ordinary life.

At Mlékojedy in Bohemia, a studied sample contained 3,568 animal bones from 122 excavated features. Only 3.2 percent belonged to wild species. Cattle, pigs and sheep or goats dominated, giving a very different picture from a diet supplied chiefly by heroic hunting expeditions.

sections.title: Skilled hands and time to play

items.text: Local potters made vessels by hand and decorated some with a small toothed wheel rolled across the clay. Fine tableware could have a dark, almost metallic-looking surface. Practical containers offered scope for careful finish and recognizable patterns as well as holding food.

A workshop at Hoštice in central Bohemia produced bone gaming dice during the Roman period. Bone and antler also supplied combs, clothing pins and sewing needles. The dice are a small reminder that life included games alongside the work needed to keep a household running.

Trade crossed the Danube frontier: Germanic visitors reached Roman markets and Roman traders travelled inland. War interrupted these relationships, especially in the Marcomannic conflicts of 166 to 180 CE. The frontier was a place of bargaining and diplomacy as well as armies.

At Mušov in southern Moravia, Roman military buildings had underfloor heating. Hot air from a furnace passed beneath floors supported on little brick pillars. The small bath complex probably served senior personnel privately; it does not show that nearby village families all enjoyed heated bathrooms.

Mušov also preserves foundation trenches of a building identified by its plan as a Roman military hospital, about 71 by 42 meters. Rooms surrounded a courtyard and communicating corridors. This evidence concerns care within an occupying army, not a documented public health service for the surrounding population.

An original Latin writing sample from Mušov is “LEGXGPF”, stamped on Roman bricks and tiles. It abbreviates Legio X Gemina Pia Fidelis, the Tenth Twin Legion, Pious and Faithful. The maker’s mark links construction materials to the legion’s brickworks at Vindobona, modern Vienna.

A corroded lump from a Roman ditch at Mušov turned out, under a CT scan, to contain two iron leg guards nested together. Both protected left legs and were different sizes. They were not a matching pair, an ancient equipment puzzle solved without pretending every lump of rust is obvious.

The Roman historian Velleius Paterculus wrote “quam incolebat Maroboduus”, meaning “which Maroboduus inhabited”, when explaining the name Boiohaemum. These are Latin words preserved through literary manuscripts and a modern edition. They are an outsider’s description, not a sample of the inhabitants’ own spoken language.

Rome prepared an expedition against Maroboduus in 6 CE, but the campaign was abandoned. He remained an important political figure until he was driven out in 19 CE and went into Roman exile. His alliances should not be stretched into the map’s entire three-century interval.

ending.text: Maroboduus lost power in 19 CE. Much later, Roman forces withdrew toward the Danube in 180 CE after another period of war. Neither event ended regional community life, and 300 CE is an imported map cutoff rather than a documented fall of “Boihaenum.”
